I’m a big proponent of analytics *in conjunction with human judgment* We throw around “analytics” too loosely. It’s become an umbrella term that’s so often used wrong and misunderstood, but I also understand why players push back…Numbers, graphs, and spreadsheets are sometimes treated as if they’re omniscient, but they’re not. What does the data say about the LeFuckYouThree? There isn’t a metric for LeBron’s attentional narrowing, decision latency, automatic motor execution, neuromuscular readiness, confidence, perceived effort, fatigue, adrenaline, crowd noise, or how the previous possessions changed his internal state. Yet we all know it’s going in, Bron too. Can analytics isolate that exact psychological and physiological state? Not really. The only person with direct access to that information is the player. Basketball IQ is built over decades of learning to read one’s self, teammates, opponents, and the constantly changing physiological state of the game. We just use the terms “rhythm” and “chemistry” and “instincts” for what the data fails to capture You can de-program players to rigidly follow a system that’s “optimal” over the course of a season, but what about game to game? Play to play? What about when you’ve missed 27 straight 3s? Or sprain your ankle? Or sprain your anke, but it’s only grade 1? Or it’s a high ankle sprain from a player diving into your legs but you need 3 points to extend your 10 point scoring streak and still have adrenaline on your side and you’re about to take a 3? Analytics can estimate expected value from historical data. Players continuously update expected value in real time using information that none of our models can fully observe. That balance is needed. Players hold incredibly valuable data that analytics cannot fully harness. And analytics hold data that can improve human judgment.
